Correspondence: {fuqingxu.fqx, liuboyin.lby, taoshuchang.tsc, liuzhaoyang.lzy, dingbolin.dbl}@alibaba-inc.com Boyin Liu Shuchang Tao Zhaoyang Liu Bolin Ding Affiliation: [1em] Tongyi Lab, Alibaba Group Abstract We present AgentJet , a distributed swarm training framework for large language model (LLM) agent reinforcement learning. Unlike centralized frameworks that tightly couple agent rollouts with model optimization, AgentJet adopts a decoupled multi-node architecture in which swarm server nodes host trainable models and run optimization on GPU clusters, whereas swarm client nodes execute arbitrary agents on arbitrary devices. This design provides capabilities that are difficult to support in centralized frameworks: (1) heterogeneous multi-model reinforcement learning, enabling the training of heterogeneous multi-agent teams with multiple LLM as brains; (2) multi-task cocktail training with isolated agent runtimes; (3) fault-tolerant execution that prevents external environment failures from interrupting the training process; and (4) live code iteration, which allows agents to be edited during training by replacing swarm client nodes. To support efficient RL in multi-model, multi-turn, and multi-agent settings, AgentJet introduces a context tracking module with timeline merging, which consolidates redundant context and achieves a 1.5–10 × \times training speedup. Finally, AgentJet introduces an automated research system that takes a research topic as input and autonomously conducts long-horizon, multi-day RL studies on large-scale clusters. By leveraging the swarm architecture, this system reproduces key exploratory workflows of RL researchers without human intervention during execution. 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) have evolved from static text generators into autonomous agents capable of multi-turn reasoning, tool invocation ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Schick et al., 2023 ) , and complex workflow execution ( OpenAI, 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) . Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a central paradigm for developing these capabilities: DeepSeek-R1 ( Guo et al., 2025 ) demonstrated that advanced reasoning behaviors, including self-reflection, verification, and dynamic strategy adaptation, can emerge through RL without supervised fine-tuning, while the OpenAI o1 series pioneered inference-time scaling through chain-of-thought reasoning ( Wei et al., 2022 ) trained with large-scale RL ( OpenAI, 2024 ) . As models transition from single-turn reasoning to long-horizon agentic tasks such as coding across entire repositories ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) , navigating web browsers ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Deng et al., 2023 ) , and orchestrating office workflows, the demands on RL training infrastructure have become correspondingly more complex. A rich ecosystem of RL training frameworks has emerged to meet this challenge. General-purpose RLHF frameworks such as OpenRLHF ( Hu et al., 2024 ) and veRL (HybridFlow) ( Sheng et al., 2024 ) have established efficient distributed architectures for post-training LLMs. OpenRLHF pioneered a Ray ( Moritz et al., 2018 ) + vLLM ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) distributed architecture that orchestrates actor, reward, reference, and critic models across GPU clusters with hybrid engine scheduling. veRL introduced a hybrid single-controller/multi-controller programming model that decouples RL control flow from computation flow, achieving state-of-the-art throughput across PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) , GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , and other algorithms. However, training agentic models, in which the LLM must interact with external environments over multiple turns, invoke tools, manage context, and coordinate with other agents, introduces qualitatively different challenges that general-purpose RLHF frameworks were not designed to address. Agentic RL trajectories are orders of magnitude longer than single-turn reasoning chains, involve heterogeneous external environments such as code sandboxes, browsers, and APIs, and exhibit high variance in completion times. These demands have catalyzed a new wave of agent-native RL frameworks. Forge by MiniMax ( MiniMax, 2026 ) introduces a middleware abstraction layer that fully decouples the training-inference engine from the agent scaffolding, treating agents as black boxes. AReaL ( Fu et al., 2025 ) pioneered fully asynchronous training-inference decoupling, achieving 3–5 × \times speedup in agent search scenarios. Agent Lightning ( Luo et al., 2025 ) converts agent experience into state-action-reward transitions that can be consumed by any RL algorithm. OpenTinker ( Zhu & You, 2026 ) advances the separation-of-concerns paradigm with a Reinforcement Learning as a Service (RLaaS) architecture. OpenClaw-RL ( Wang et al., 2026 ) explores every agent interaction as a live training signal for continuous online policy optimization. Despite this rapid progress, existing frameworks share several critical limitations when applied to real-world LLM agent training: • Runtime Fragility: Most frameworks assume that agent rollout environments and model training coexist within the same cluster. When an agent requires specific dependencies, such as Docker containers, browser automation, or database connections, a single component failure can crash the entire training pipeline and lose all progress since the last checkpoint. • Debugging Friction: Modifying agent code or reward functions requires restarting the entire training process, including expensive model loading and vLLM initialization, resulting in 5–10 minute iteration cycles. • Multi-Model Constraints: Current systems predominantly optimize a single policy model, while real-world agentic applications increasingly involve heterogeneous multi-agent systems where different agents use models of different sizes (e.g., 7B for execution, 32B for planning). • Redundant Context: As agents interact with environments over many turns, conversation contexts accumulate substantial redundancy (repeated system prompts, tool definitions, and observation histories), leading to wasted computation during policy gradient updates. • Environment Lock-in: Multi-task cocktail training simultaneously trains on tasks with incompatible runtime dependencies and therefore requires strong isolation between task environments, which monolithic architectures struggle to provide. In this paper, we introduce AgentJet , a distributed swarm training framework that addresses these challenges through a fundamental architectural innovation: the complete decoupling of agent runtime from training infrastructure via a client-server paradigm. Our contributions are: 1. Swarm Architecture (Section 3 ): A flexible client-server paradigm that supports fault-tolerant training, hot-swap debugging, heterogeneous multi-model RL, multi-task cocktail training, and a timeline merging algorithm that achieves 1.5–10 × \times speedup. 2. Swarm Training Capabilities (Section 5 ): We demonstrate two higher-level workflows enabled by the swarm architecture: vibe training , in which AI coding assistants generate complete training code from natural language specifications, and benchmark evaluations across diverse agentic tasks. 3. Automated Research Pipelines (Section 6 ): A fully autonomous system in which an AI research agent plans, executes, and analyzes multi-day experimental campaigns, validated through six independent case studies spanning hyperparameter optimization, model scale comparison, and LoRA configuration analysis. AgentJet is fully open-source and framework-agnostic, supporting integration with LangChain, AgentScope, raw HTTP endpoints, and any agent scaffolding that can issue LLM inference requests. 2 Related Work 2.1 Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for LLMs The rapid development of LLM-based agents has produced a rich landscape of RL training frameworks, which we organize along two axes: general-purpose RLHF systems and agent-native RL systems. General-Purpose RLHF Frameworks. OpenRLHF ( Hu et al., 2024 ) pioneered a Ray ( Moritz et al., 2018 ) + vLLM ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) distributed architecture that orchestrates actor, reward, reference, and critic models across GPU clusters with hybrid engine scheduling. veRL (HybridFlow) ( Sheng et al., 2024 ) introduced a hybrid single-controller/multi-controller programming model that decouples RL control flow from computation flow, achieving state-of-the-art throughput across PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) , GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , and other algorithms. These frameworks have been instrumental in scaling reasoning RL; however, they were designed primarily for single-turn or short-horizon interactions and assume tightly coupled training-inference environments. Agent-Native RL Frameworks. A new wave of frameworks has emerged to address the specific demands of agentic training. Forge by MiniMax ( MiniMax, 2026 ) introduces a middleware abstraction that treats agents as black boxes whose LLM requests are routed through a service gateway, and it integrates Context Management as an explicit agent action within the RL loop to mitigate context rot. AReaL ( Fu et al., 2025 ) , jointly developed by Tsinghua University and Ant Group, pioneered fully asynchronous training-inference decoupling, achieving 3–5 × \times speedup; the v1.0 release introduced Proxy Worker middleware that enables any agent to connect to RL training with a single API endpoint change. Agent Lightning ( Luo et al., 2025 ) from Microsoft Research converts agent experience into state-action-reward transitions, enabling low-intrusion integration with existing frameworks. OpenTinker ( Zhu & You, 2026 ) advances the separation-of-concerns paradigm with a Reinforcement Learning as a Service (RLaaS) architecture and an Agent Protocol Coordinator for multi-agent training. OpenClaw-RL ( Wang et al., 2026 ) treats every agent interaction as a live training signal for continuous online policy optimization. Compared with these systems, AgentJet provides: (1) complete decoupling of training and inference across arbitrary devices with a many-to-many topology, (2) heterogeneous multi-model multi-agent RL without parameter sharing, (3) architecture-level fault tolerance in which client failures cannot interrupt training, (4) timeline merging for efficient multi-turn training with 1.5–10 × \times speedup, and (5) framework-agnostic black-box agent support that requires zero code modifications. 2.2 Automated Scientific Research The vision of AI-conducted research has advanced rapidly. AI Scientist from Sakana AI ( Lu et al., 2024 ) demonstrated end-to-end automated research, from idea generation through code implementation, experimentation, paper writing, and peer review. AI Co-Scientist from Google DeepMind ( Gottweis et al., 2025 ) further explored AI-driven scientific hypothesis generation and experimental design. AI-Researcher ( Tang et al., 2025 ) from HKU received a NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight. AgentRxiv ( Schmidgall & Moor, 2025 ) employs multi-agent collaboration to iteratively improve results, increasing MATH-500 ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ; Lightman et al., 2024 ) accuracy from 70.2% to 78.2% through automated research cycles.
